screens.title: Variables and Assignment: Naming Values
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will learn what a variable is, how Python assigns values, and why naming choices matter. A variable is simply a name that refers to a value stored in memory. Learning to write clear assignment statements — using the assignment operator, spoken as equals — helps you keep programs readable and predictable. You will see how assignment differs from mathematical equality, why names must follow rules like starting with a letter or underscore, and why conventions such as snake_case and ALL_CAPS for constants improve communication. We will practice reassignment, multiple assignment and swapping so you can manipulate values safely. Along the way I will show the memory-as-label idea: variables are references or tags pointing to values, not physical boxes that contain them. That difference matters when you share or reassign complex values. By the end, you should be able to write valid variable names, explain why x equals five assigns rather than states a math fact, and swap two variables without a temporary placeholder. Notice how these basics let you name and move data confidently across programs. What variable will you create first?

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Variables and Assignment

Variables and Assignment: Naming Values

Understand how names refer to data, how assignment works in Python, and the naming rules and conventions that make code readable.

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
In this lesson
What is a variable?
A name that refers to a value stored in memory. It helps you reuse and update data.
Assignment vs equality

Naming rules & conventions

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this lesson you will meet four concrete objectives that move you from recognition to practical use. First, you will be able to explain what a variable is and how it refers to a value in memory. This means describing the label-and-container analogy and why Python treats names as references. Second, you will write assignment statements using the equals operator to store values in names, and you will understand that assignment is an action, not a mathematical equality. Third, you will name variables according to Python rules and conventions: valid characters, no leading digits, case sensitivity, avoiding reserved words, and using snake_case and descriptive names. Fourth, you will understand reassignment and references: how changing a variable binds the name to a new object and why that matters for lists and complex types. Each objective combines a definition, quick practice example, and a short check so you can show the skill to someone else. These skills let you create clear, correct code and avoid common beginner errors. Which objective will you try first in the hands-on exercises?

screens.title: What is a variable?
screens.narratorSegment: Start by defining a variable: it is a name you give to a value so you can refer to that value later. Think of a warehouse shelf filled with objects. The objects are values; variable names are the tags you attach to those objects to find and use them. This naming makes code easier to write and read because you do not need to remember memory addresses. A concrete example: when you bind the name x to the number five, you can later use the name x in arithmetic or printing and Python will look up the value five. A common misconception is to treat variables as boxes that hold values and change the contents; in Python, names are references that point to objects. Reassignment moves the reference to a different object rather than changing the original object. For simple immutable types like numbers and strings, this difference is mostly invisible, but it matters with lists and other mutable types. Key takeaway: use clear names to express intent and remember that a variable is the label, not the object itself. How does this label idea change how you think about updating data in your programs?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A variable is a name that refers to a value stored somewhere in memory; use names to refer to values instead of remembering memory details.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › What is a variable?
Label-on-box analogy

Variables are tags or names attached to values. The values live as objects in memory; variable names point to them so you can reuse or update references without handling raw memory addresses.

Concrete example
# bind name x to number five
x = 5
print(x)  # prints 5

# later, reassign x to a new value
x = 10
print(x)  # prints 10
Common misconception
A variable is not a container that mutates. Reassignment binds the name to a new object instead of modifying the previous object.
Key takeaway
Think labels and references. That mental model avoids many confusion points later.
Memory sketch
Objects
5
10
"Hello"
Names (references)
x points to 5
greeting points to Hello

screens.title: Assignment statements
screens.narratorSegment: Assignment connects a name on the left to a value on the right using the assignment operator, spoken as equals. Concretely, when you execute the line x equals five, Python evaluates the right-hand expression, creates or locates the value object, and then binds the name x to that object. This is an action, not a mathematical statement. A helpful example to practice: assign x equals five, then assign x equals x plus one. The second line reads the current value bound to x, adds one, and assigns the result back to x. In the interpreter you will see the printed values change accordingly. A common beginner error is trying to write five equals x; that fails because the left side must be a writable name, not a literal. Another useful pattern is assigning different types into the same name: x can hold an integer, then later hold a string. That flexibility, called dynamic typing, is powerful but requires you to track types carefully. Try the example in the code panel and notice each assignment is an action that updates which object the name refers to. What does that imply when you later reuse the name in calculations?

keyIdea.title: Assignment
keyIdea.text: Use the assignment operator to bind names to values; assignment evaluates the right side and stores the resulting object under the name on the left.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Assignment statements
Explain the action of assignment

Assignment evaluates the right-hand expression, creates or locates the object, and binds the left-hand name to that object. It is an action performed by the interpreter.

Interactive code example
x = 5
print(x)    # prints 5
x = x + 1   # read current x, add 1, assign back
print(x)    # prints 6
x = "done"
print(x)    # prints done
Common mistake
Writing a literal on the left, for example five equals x, causes a syntax error because literals are not valid assignment targets.
Notes and rules
  • Left side must be a valid name or writable target.
  • Right side is evaluated first, then bound to the name on the left.
  • Assignment is not equality; it describes an action the interpreter performs.
Check your understanding
Try assigning a name to different types and printing results. Notice how the name's referent changes with each assignment.

screens.title: Assignment vs Mathematical Equality
screens.narratorSegment: Students often confuse the assignment operator with mathematical equality. In mathematics an equals sign asserts that two expressions represent the same value. In programming assignment is an action that stores a value under a name. For example, x equals five is interpreted as bind name x to the value five. Writing x equals x plus one is valid in code because it reads the current value of x, computes a new value, and then stores the result back into x. Mathematically that would be a contradictory statement, but in programming it is an update operation. A common error from this confusion is attempting to assign into a literal, like five equals x; the interpreter raises a syntax error because the left-hand side is not a valid name. Another important difference is that assignment has order: the right side is evaluated before the binding occurs. Understanding this contrast clears up why assignment statements can change program state and why they must follow syntactic rules. Reflect: how would you explain this difference to a peer using the label-on-box analogy? Assignment vs Mathematical Equality means assignment stores a value under a name and changes program state; mathematical equality asserts a relationship and does not perform assignment.. In practical terms, why equals in code is an action, not a statement of equality. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Assignment vs Equality
Side-by-side
Mathematics: equals asserts both sides are the same value. It is a statement to be proven or used in algebra.
Programming: assignment is an action that stores the result of the right-hand expression under the left-hand name.
Code example to try in interpreter: assign a variable, then update it using an expression involving the same variable to observe state change.
Concrete example
count = 5
count = count + 1
print(count)  # prints 6

# invalid in Python:
# 5 = count  -> SyntaxError
Misconception
Treating assignment like an algebraic equality leads to invalid code and logic errors. Remember: assignment changes program state.

screens.title: Python naming rules
screens.narratorSegment: Python enforces specific rules for variable names so the interpreter can parse code correctly. Names may contain letters, digits and underscores. They cannot start with a digit, so a name like two_places starting with a number would be invalid. Names are case-sensitive, meaning Name, name and NAME are distinct names. Also you cannot use Python reserved words such as if, for, while, class, def, or print as variable names because those words have special meaning in the language. These are syntactic requirements, not stylistic choices, and violating them results in syntax errors. A simple exercise is to try several names in the interpreter and observe the error messages. A useful habit is to choose descriptive names using lowercase and underscores. That both follows the rules and helps readers of your code understand intent. Finally, using meaningful names reduces bugs because the name communicates the role of the value. What descriptive name will you pick for storing the number of items in a list? Python naming rules means valid names use letters, digits and underscores; cannot start with a digit; are case-sensitive; and must not be reserved words.. In practical terms, what characters are allowed and what is forbidden. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Valid names use letters, digits and underscores; cannot start with a digit; are case-sensitive; and must not be reserved words.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Python naming rules
Rules checklist
  • Allowed: letters, digits, underscore.
  • Not allowed: start with a digit — 2nd_place is invalid.
  • Case-sensitive: Name and name are different.
  • Cannot use reserved words like if, for, while, class, def, print.
Try this
city = "Atlanta"
temperature1 = 72
# invalid: 2nd_place = 5  -> SyntaxError
# invalid: class = "math"  -> SyntaxError
Why rules matter

Following naming rules prevents syntax errors and ensures the interpreter can parse your code. They also make your code portable and consistent with the wider Python community.

Small exercise
Create five variable names you will use in a small program, then confirm each is accepted by the interpreter.

screens.title: Naming conventions: snake_case and descriptiveness
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond rules, conventions guide how you name variables so other programmers — and your future self — can understand intent. In Python, the common style for variable names is snake_case: lowercase words separated by underscores. Use descriptive names such as hours_worked, total_score, or number_of_items instead of vague letters like h or n. Short single-letter names are acceptable only as conventional loop counters like i, j, and k or when used in brief mathematical contexts. Descriptive names reveal intent and make maintenance easier. For example, temperature_celsius is clearer than t. Another convention is to use ALL_CAPS for names that are intended as constants, indicating they should not be changed. Remember these are conventions, not enforced by the interpreter; they are social agreements that improve readability and collaboration. When naming, ask: does this name tell a reader what kind of value or role the variable has? If not, choose a clearer name. Naming conventions: snake_case and descriptiveness means prefer snake_case and descriptive names; reserve single letters for conventional, short-lived roles and use all_caps for intended constants.. In practical terms, how to choose readable names for variables. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Naming conventions
Snake_case examples
  • student_name
  • total_score
  • number_of_items
When to use short names
Use i, j, k for short loop counters or well-known mathematical variables like x and y in small, clear contexts.
ALL_CAPS for constants
Use uppercase names to signal that a value is intended as a constant, for example PI or MAX_USERS. Python will not enforce immutability, but this communicates intent to other programmers.
Quick practice
Rename a variable in a small snippet to show how clearer names make code easier to follow.

screens.title: Variables as references
screens.narratorSegment: A key concept in Python is that variables are references to objects in memory. When you assign y equals x, you do not copy the object; you create a new name y that refers to the same object x refers to. For immutable objects like integers and strings this detail is often invisible, but for mutable objects like lists it is crucial: changing the object through one name is visible through the other name because both refer to the same object. For example, if you assign list_a to a list object and then set list_b equals list_a, both names refer to the same list. Appending to list_b will show the change when you inspect list_a. A common misunderstanding is to assume assignment makes a deep copy; it does not. If you want a separate object you must explicitly copy it. Practice by assigning a list to two names and mutating it, then observe the shared state. The takeaway: understand whether you are working with references or independent copies before mutating values. Variables as references means assigning one name to another makes both names refer to the same object; mutations via one name are visible through the other.. In practical terms, names point to objects; multiple names can refer to the same object. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: References
keyIdea.text: Assigning one name to another makes both names refer to the same object; mutations via one name are visible through the other.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Variables as references
Example with a list
list_a = [1, 2, 3]
list_b = list_a
list_b.append(4)
print(list_a)  # prints [1, 2, 3, 4]
print(list_b)  # prints [1, 2, 3, 4]
This demonstrates that list_a and list_b refer to the same object. Mutating the object through one name is visible to the other name because they both point to the same memory object.
Contrast
If you need an independent copy, explicitly copy the object rather than assign the name. Assignment alone does not make a separate object.
Check
Assign a list to two names, mutate one, and confirm both show the change. Then make a copy and confirm independent mutation.

screens.title: Reassignment and dynamic typing
screens.narratorSegment: Reassignment is the act of giving a name a new value. Python is dynamically typed, meaning a name can refer to different types at different times. For example, x can be an integer, then later a string. Reassignment creates or locates the new object and updates the name to point to it. This is safe and flexible, but it requires discipline: you must track the expected type when writing and reading code. Many bugs arise when a name is used with an unexpected type. A simple process to keep code clear: choose descriptive names that suggest the type or role, reassign sparingly in long functions, and write short, focused blocks where the type of a name remains stable. Concrete example: set x equals five, reassign x equals ten, then reassign x equals the greeting Hello. Try these in the interpreter to see the printed outputs change. A good habit is to add comments or use distinct names when a variable changes role drastically. How will you track types in your code to avoid confusion? Reassignment and dynamic typing means reassignment binds a name to a new object. python allows different types over time, so track names' roles to avoid type confusion.. screens.title: Constants and ALL_CAPS convention

screens.title: Common naming and assignment mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Beginners commonly make a handful of naming and assignment mistakes that are easy to avoid with a small checklist. First, starting a name with a digit triggers a syntax error; always begin names with a letter or underscore. Second, using reserved words like class or def as variable names causes parsing errors; consult the list of Python keywords if uncertain. Third, confusing assignment with equality leads to attempts to assign into a literal, which fails. Fourth, poor naming — single-letter names outside conventional uses — makes code hard to read and maintain. Fifth, misunderstanding references leads to unexpected shared mutations when working with mutable types like lists. To avoid these, follow three practical rules: choose descriptive snake_case names, run small checks in the interpreter to read error messages, and when sharing or mutating objects consider whether you need a copy. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will learn what a variable is, how Python assigns values, and why naming choices matter. A variable is simply a name that refers to a value stored in memory. Learning to write clear assignment statements — using the assignment operator, spoken as equals — helps you keep programs readable and predictable. You will see how assignment differs from mathematical equality, why names must follow rules like starting with a letter or underscore, and why conventions such as snake_case and ALL_CAPS for constants improve communication. We will practice reassignment, multiple assignment and swapping so you can manipulate values safely. Along the way I will show the memory-as-label idea: variables are references or tags pointing to values, not physical boxes that contain them. That difference matters when you share or reassign complex values. By the end, you should be able to write valid variable names, explain why x equals five assigns rather than states a math fact, and swap two variables without a temporary placeholder. Notice how these basics let you name and move data confidently across programs. What variable will you create first?

By the end of this lesson you will meet four concrete objectives that move you from recognition to practical use. First, you will be able to explain what a variable is and how it refers to a value in memory. This means describing the label-and-container analogy and why Python treats names as references. Second, you will write assignment statements using the equals operator to store values in names, and you will understand that assignment is an action, not a mathematical equality. Third, you will name variables according to Python rules and conventions: valid characters, no leading digits, case sensitivity, avoiding reserved words, and using snake_case and descriptive names. Fourth, you will understand reassignment and references: how changing a variable binds the name to a new object and why that matters for lists and complex types. Each objective combines a definition, quick practice example, and a short check so you can show the skill to someone else. These skills let you create clear, correct code and avoid common beginner errors. Which objective will you try first in the hands-on exercises?

These practice goals translate the objectives into quick checks you can use while coding. For explaining variables, describe the label-on-box analogy and give an example such as a name equal to five. For assignment statements, write three short lines that store numbers and strings using the assignment operator, and run them to confirm printed output. For naming rules and conventions, produce five valid and descriptive variable names and one invalid name that starts with a digit, then note the error you see. For references and reassignment, demonstrate reassignment and multiple assignment, including swapping two variables using tuple unpacking. Each check is designed so you can show the behavior in a Python interpreter, read the error messages, and explain why they occur. These small checks build confidence and make it easy to demonstrate competency to a peer or instructor. Which check will you run first in the interpreter?

Start by defining a variable: it is a name you give to a value so you can refer to that value later. Think of a warehouse shelf filled with objects. The objects are values; variable names are the tags you attach to those objects to find and use them. This naming makes code easier to write and read because you do not need to remember memory addresses. A concrete example: when you bind the name x to the number five, you can later use the name x in arithmetic or printing and Python will look up the value five. A common misconception is to treat variables as boxes that hold values and change the contents; in Python, names are references that point to objects. Reassignment moves the reference to a different object rather than changing the original object. For simple immutable types like numbers and strings, this difference is mostly invisible, but it matters with lists and other mutable types. Key takeaway: use clear names to express intent and remember that a variable is the label, not the object itself. How does this label idea change how you think about updating data in your programs?

Assignment connects a name on the left to a value on the right using the assignment operator, spoken as equals. Concretely, when you execute the line x equals five, Python evaluates the right-hand expression, creates or locates the value object, and then binds the name x to that object. This is an action, not a mathematical statement. A helpful example to practice: assign x equals five, then assign x equals x plus one. The second line reads the current value bound to x, adds one, and assigns the result back to x. In the interpreter you will see the printed values change accordingly. A common beginner error is trying to write five equals x; that fails because the left side must be a writable name, not a literal. Another useful pattern is assigning different types into the same name: x can hold an integer, then later hold a string. That flexibility, called dynamic typing, is powerful but requires you to track types carefully. Try the example in the code panel and notice each assignment is an action that updates which object the name refers to. What does that imply when you later reuse the name in calculations?

Students often confuse the assignment operator with mathematical equality. In mathematics an equals sign asserts that two expressions represent the same value. In programming assignment is an action that stores a value under a name. For example, x equals five is interpreted as bind name x to the value five. Writing x equals x plus one is valid in code because it reads the current value of x, computes a new value, and then stores the result back into x. Mathematically that would be a contradictory statement, but in programming it is an update operation. A common error from this confusion is attempting to assign into a literal, like five equals x; the interpreter raises a syntax error because the left-hand side is not a valid name. Another important difference is that assignment has order: the right side is evaluated before the binding occurs. Understanding this contrast clears up why assignment statements can change program state and why they must follow syntactic rules. Reflect: how would you explain this difference to a peer using the label-on-box analogy? Assignment vs Mathematical Equality means assignment stores a value under a name and changes program state; mathematical equality asserts a relationship and does not perform assignment.. In practical terms, why equals in code is an action, not a statement of equality. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Python enforces specific rules for variable names so the interpreter can parse code correctly. Names may contain letters, digits and underscores. They cannot start with a digit, so a name like two_places starting with a number would be invalid. Names are case-sensitive, meaning Name, name and NAME are distinct names. Also you cannot use Python reserved words such as if, for, while, class, def, or print as variable names because those words have special meaning in the language. These are syntactic requirements, not stylistic choices, and violating them results in syntax errors. A simple exercise is to try several names in the interpreter and observe the error messages. A useful habit is to choose descriptive names using lowercase and underscores. That both follows the rules and helps readers of your code understand intent. Finally, using meaningful names reduces bugs because the name communicates the role of the value. What descriptive name will you pick for storing the number of items in a list? Python naming rules means valid names use letters, digits and underscores; cannot start with a digit; are case-sensitive; and must not be reserved words.. In practical terms, what characters are allowed and what is forbidden. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Beyond rules, conventions guide how you name variables so other programmers — and your future self — can understand intent. In Python, the common style for variable names is snake_case: lowercase words separated by underscores. Use descriptive names such as hours_worked, total_score, or number_of_items instead of vague letters like h or n. Short single-letter names are acceptable only as conventional loop counters like i, j, and k or when used in brief mathematical contexts. Descriptive names reveal intent and make maintenance easier. For example, temperature_celsius is clearer than t. Another convention is to use ALL_CAPS for names that are intended as constants, indicating they should not be changed. Remember these are conventions, not enforced by the interpreter; they are social agreements that improve readability and collaboration. When naming, ask: does this name tell a reader what kind of value or role the variable has? If not, choose a clearer name. Naming conventions: snake_case and descriptiveness means prefer snake_case and descriptive names; reserve single letters for conventional, short-lived roles and use all_caps for intended constants.. In practical terms, how to choose readable names for variables. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A key concept in Python is that variables are references to objects in memory. When you assign y equals x, you do not copy the object; you create a new name y that refers to the same object x refers to. For immutable objects like integers and strings this detail is often invisible, but for mutable objects like lists it is crucial: changing the object through one name is visible through the other name because both refer to the same object. For example, if you assign list_a to a list object and then set list_b equals list_a, both names refer to the same list. Appending to list_b will show the change when you inspect list_a. A common misunderstanding is to assume assignment makes a deep copy; it does not. If you want a separate object you must explicitly copy it. Practice by assigning a list to two names and mutating it, then observe the shared state. The takeaway: understand whether you are working with references or independent copies before mutating values. Variables as references means assigning one name to another makes both names refer to the same object; mutations via one name are visible through the other.. In practical terms, names point to objects; multiple names can refer to the same object. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Reassignment is the act of giving a name a new value. Python is dynamically typed, meaning a name can refer to different types at different times. For example, x can be an integer, then later a string. Reassignment creates or locates the new object and updates the name to point to it. Beginners commonly make a handful of naming and assignment mistakes that are easy to avoid with a small checklist. First, starting a name with a digit triggers a syntax error; always begin names with a letter or underscore. Second, using reserved words like class or def as variable names causes parsing errors; consult the list of Python keywords if uncertain. Third, confusing assignment with equality leads to attempts to assign into a literal, which fails. Fourth, poor naming — single-letter names outside conventional uses — makes code hard to read and maintain. Third, assignment is not mathematical equality and has an order: the right-hand side is evaluated before binding. These three cover the core behavior. Fourth, Python naming rules permit letters, digits and underscore, but names cannot start with a digit and are case-sensitive. Fifth, follow conventions like snake_case and descriptive names to make code readable.
